text_excerpt: Profile --> Steve Dow Studies CAR T cell Immunotherapy for Treatment of Metastatic Osteosarcoma in Dogs CAR T cells for Metastatic Osteosarcoma CAR T cell Immunotherapy for Treatment of Metastatic Osteosarcoma in Dogs CAR T cells for Metastatic Osteosarcoma Osteosarcoma (OS) is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma that have macroscopic metastases to the lungs. CAR (chimeric antigen receptor) T cells are a modified version of a T cell, a type of immune cell, that alters them so they can target and destroy cancer cells. Dogs have been previously treated with CAR (chimeric antigen receptor) T cells at other institutions and the treatment has been well-tolerated, but the new CAR T cells being evaluated in this trial have not been evaluated in dogs with cancer, though safety studies were done in healthy dogs, without side effects. The goal of this study is to determine the safety and effectiveness of canine CAR T cells, which will be generated by gene modification of your dogs white blood cells, and then infused back into your dog by an intravenous catheter. In order to help the CAR T cells expand in the body more effectively, your dog will also have to be treated with bone marrow suppressing drugs (fludarabine and cyclophosphamide) for 2 days before the CAR T cells are given back. To help increase the effectiveness of the CAR T cells once they are recruited to the tumor tissues, dogs will be treated daily with oral losartan and propranolol before and after CAR T administration.
